Differentially Private PCA Visualizations

Source: vignettes/theory-dp-visualization.Rmd
theory-dp-visualization.Rmd

The dppca package combines private PC directions, private variance estimates along those directions, and private score histograms to construct five PCA visualizations: scree, loading, score, variable, and biplot. This article describes how these visualizations are constructed from DP estimates, what information each plot represents, and how their interpretations differ from those of ordinary PCA. Particular attention is given to the DP variable plot and biplot, which combine multiple private quantities.

For background on ordinary PCA visualizations, see PCA Background. The underlying DP estimation methods are described in Theory of DP Loading, Theory of DP Scree, and Theory of DP Score. For implementation details, plotting options, and examples, see the DP PCA Visualization Tutorial.

1. What is estimated privately?

Let X∈ℝn×pX\in\mathbb R^{n\times p} contain observations x1,…,xn∈ℝpx_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p in its rows. For clarity, suppose that dp_pca() retains the first kk components and displays two selected axes axes = c(a, b), with a≠ba\ne b and a,b∈{1,…,k}a,b\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.

The integrated procedure uses the following quantities:

Quantity Notation Role
DP PC directions Ṽ=(ṽ1,…,ṽp)\widetilde V=(\widetilde v_1,\ldots,\widetilde v_p) Define the common PC axes and loading coefficients.
DP eigenvalues λ̃1,…,λ̃k\widetilde\lambda_1,\ldots,\widetilde\lambda_k Determine scree/PVE and scale variable and biplot coordinates.
DP score frame F̃\widetilde F Defines the two-dimensional plotting region.
DP score histogram h̃\widetilde h Describes the distribution of projected observations without releasing individual coordinates.
Synthetic score points s1*,…,sN*s_1^*,\ldots,s_N^* Provide a point-based view sampled from h̃\widetilde h.

The mathematical definitions and estimation procedures for these quantities are described in the corresponding articles: Theory of DP Loading for DP PC directions, Theory of DP Scree for DP eigenvalues, and Theory of DP Score for the DP score frame, histogram, and synthetic score sampling. These five quantities are used to construct five DP PCA visualizations: scree, loading, score, variable, and biplot.

2. Privacy budget and shared estimation

Write the total privacy budget as (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta). The integrated procedure requires allocations for loading, scree, and score: εL+εS+εscore=ε,δL+δS+δscore=δ. \begin{aligned} \varepsilon_L+\varepsilon_S+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}&=\varepsilon,\\ \delta_L+\delta_S+\delta_{\mathrm{score}}&=\delta. \end{aligned}

Within the score allocation, the package uses

εF=0.35εscore,δF=0,εH=0.65εscore,δH=δscore, \begin{aligned} \varepsilon_F&=0.35\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}, &\delta_F&=0,\\ \varepsilon_H&=0.65\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}, &\delta_H&=\delta_{\mathrm{score}}, \end{aligned}

where FF denotes the private frame and HH the private histogram. The frame budget is shared equally among two private coordinate medians and a private radial quantile.

The resulting estimation flow is X→Ṽ(loading budget),(X,Ṽ)→λ̃1:k(scree budget),(X,Ṽ)→F̃→h̃(score budget),(Ṽ,λ̃1:k,F̃,h̃)→five PCA displays. \begin{gathered} X\ \longrightarrow\ \widetilde V\quad\text{(loading budget)},\\ (X,\widetilde V)\ \longrightarrow\ \widetilde\lambda_{1:k}\quad\text{(scree budget)},\\ (X,\widetilde V)\ \longrightarrow\ \widetilde F\ \longrightarrow\ \widetilde h \quad\text{(score budget)},\\ (\widetilde V,\widetilde\lambda_{1:k},\widetilde F,\widetilde h) \ \longrightarrow\ \text{five PCA displays}. \end{gathered}

Only one direction matrix, one selected scree method, and one selected histogram method are estimated within an integrated fit.

3. Five DP PCA Visualization

The five DP PCA visualizations are scree, loading, score, variable, and biplot. The construction of the DP scree, loading, and score plots is described in Theory of DP Loading, Theory of DP Scree, and Theory of DP Score, respectively. Therefore, this section focuses on the construction and interpretation of the DP variable plot and DP biplot.

3.1. DP variable plot (correlation-style coordinates)

In ordinary PCA, a variable plot represents the correlations between the original variables and the PC scores. As described in Section 4.4 of PCA Background, the correlation between variable jj and the ℓ\ellth PC score is

Cor(X⋅j,S⋅ℓ)=λ̂ℓv̂jℓσ̂j, \operatorname{Cor}(X_{\cdot j},S_{\cdot\ell}) = \frac{\sqrt{\widehat\lambda_\ell}\,\widehat v_{j\ell}} {\widehat\sigma_j},

where λ̂ℓ\widehat\lambda_\ell and v̂jℓ\widehat v_{j\ell} are the sample eigenvalue and loading coefficient, respectively, and σ̂j\widehat\sigma_j is the sample standard deviation of variable jj.

In the DP setting, these empirical quantities cannot be directly released without accounting for their privacy costs. Instead, dp_pca() constructs the variable plot using privately estimated PC directions and eigenvalues.

Let Ṽk=(ṽ1,…,ṽk)\widetilde V_k=(\widetilde v_1,\ldots,\widetilde v_k) denote the first kk private PC directions, and let λ̃1,…,λ̃k\widetilde\lambda_1,\ldots,\widetilde\lambda_k be the corresponding nonnegative private eigenvalues. These quantities define a DP-based covariance approximation,

Σ̃k=Ṽkdiag(λ̃1,…,λ̃k)Ṽk⊤. \widetilde\Sigma_k = \widetilde V_k \operatorname{diag} (\widetilde\lambda_1,\ldots,\widetilde\lambda_k) \widetilde V_k^\top.

Therefore, the implied variance of variable jj is

σ̃j,k2=(Σ̃k)jj=∑ℓ=1kλ̃ℓṽjℓ2. \widetilde\sigma_{j,k}^2 = (\widetilde\Sigma_k)_{jj} = \sum_{\ell=1}^{k} \widetilde\lambda_\ell\widetilde v_{j\ell}^{\,2}.

Using this quantity in place of the sample variance, we define the DP correlation coordinate of variable jj along PC ℓ\ell as

r̃jℓ=λ̃ℓṽjℓσ̃j,k,σ̃j,k>0. \widetilde r_{j\ell} = \frac{ \sqrt{\widetilde\lambda_\ell}\,\widetilde v_{j\ell} }{ \widetilde\sigma_{j,k} }, \qquad \widetilde\sigma_{j,k}>0.

For two selected components aa and bb, the DP variable plot represents variable jj by

RjDP=(r̃ja,r̃jb). R_j^{\mathrm{DP}} = (\widetilde r_{ja},\widetilde r_{jb}).

Variables with zero implied variance are omitted because their coordinates are undefined.

As in the ordinary variable plot, the DP coordinates lie inside or on the unit circle. Indeed,

∥RjDP∥22=r̃ja2+r̃jb2=λ̃aṽja2+λ̃bṽjb2∑ℓ=1kλ̃ℓṽjℓ2≤1. \|R_j^{\mathrm{DP}}\|_2^2 = \widetilde r_{ja}^{\,2} + \widetilde r_{jb}^{\,2} = \frac{ \widetilde\lambda_a\widetilde v_{ja}^{\,2} + \widetilde\lambda_b\widetilde v_{jb}^{\,2} }{ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{k} \widetilde\lambda_\ell\widetilde v_{j\ell}^{\,2} } \le 1.

The squared distance from the origin measures how much of the reconstructed variance of variable jj is attributed to the two displayed PCs, relative to all kk retained PCs. Variables near the unit circle have most of their reconstructed variance associated with the displayed PCs, whereas variables near the origin have more of their reconstructed variance associated with the other retained PCs.

The angles between variable vectors can provide information about their associations in the displayed PC plane. Vectors pointing in similar directions suggest positive associations, while vectors pointing in opposite directions suggest negative associations. Approximately perpendicular vectors indicate weak associations within the displayed plane. These interpretations are most informative when the variables are well represented by the selected components.

3.2. DP biplot

A biplot displays observations and variables simultaneously in a low-dimensional representation of the data. In ordinary PCA, as described in Section 4.5 of PCA Background, the biplot coordinates are constructed from the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the centered data matrix. For two selected components aa and bb, the observation and variable coordinates are given by

Gα=UIDI1−α,Hα=VIDIα,0≤α≤1, G_\alpha=U_ID_I^{1-\alpha}, \qquad H_\alpha=V_ID_I^\alpha, \qquad 0\le\alpha\le1,

where I={a,b}I=\{a,b\} and DI=diag(da,db)D_I=\operatorname{diag}(d_a,d_b) contains the corresponding singular values. The parameter α\alpha determines how the singular-value scaling is distributed between observations and variables.

In the DP setting, dp_pca() constructs a DP biplot using synthetic score points generated from the private score histogram, together with privately estimated PC directions and eigenvalues. Recall that the singular values in ordinary PCA satisfy dℓ=(n−1)λ̂ℓd_\ell=\sqrt{(n-1)\widehat\lambda_\ell}. Accordingly, we define the corresponding DP-based scaling factors as

d̃ℓ=(n−1)λ̃ℓ,ℓ∈{a,b}, \widetilde d_\ell = \sqrt{(n-1)\widetilde\lambda_\ell}, \qquad \ell\in\{a,b\},

where λ̃ℓ≥0\widetilde\lambda_\ell\ge0 denotes the private eigenvalues and nn is the original sample size.

Let si*=(sia*,sib*)s_i^*=(s_{ia}^*,s_{ib}^*) denote the iith synthetic score point generated from the private histogram, and let ṽjℓ\widetilde v_{j\ell} denote the coefficient of variable jj in the ℓ\ellth private PC direction. For d̃ℓ>0\widetilde d_\ell>0, the DP biplot coordinates are defined by

GiℓDP(α)=siℓ*−cℓdispd̃ℓα,HjℓDP(α)=ṽjℓd̃ℓα, G_{i\ell}^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) = \frac{s_{i\ell}^*-c_\ell^{\mathrm{disp}}} {\widetilde d_\ell^\alpha}, \qquad H_{j\ell}^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) = \widetilde v_{j\ell}\widetilde d_\ell^\alpha,

where cℓdispc_\ell^{\mathrm{disp}} is the display-centering adjustment defined in Section 8.1 of Theory of DP Score, with its two coordinates corresponding to the selected PC axes aa and bb, respectively.

With center = TRUE (the default), the synthetic scores are translated relative to the private frame center, and the variable arrows originate at (0,0)(0,0). With center = FALSE, the scores remain unshifted, and the variable arrows originate at the private frame center expressed in the alpha-transformed coordinates.

For the two selected components, the rows GiDP(α)=(GiaDP(α),GibDP(α))G_i^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) = \left( G_{ia}^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha), G_{ib}^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) \right) represent synthetic observations, while HjDP(α)=(HjaDP(α),HjbDP(α))H_j^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) = \left( H_{ja}^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha), H_{jb}^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) \right) represent the original variables through their private direction coefficients.

As in ordinary PCA, the parameter α\alpha controls the relative scaling of the observation and variable coordinates:

  • α=0\alpha=0: Observation coordinates retain the synthetic score scale (apart from optional centering), and variable coordinates are the private PC direction coefficients.
  • α=1/2\alpha=1/2: The DP-based singular-value scaling is shared symmetrically between observations and variables.
  • α=1\alpha=1: Variable coordinates are multiplied by the full DP-based singular-value factors, while synthetic score coordinates are divided by them.

Arrow scaling. To display observations and variable vectors on a common plotting region, dp_pca() applies an additional scaling factor to the variable vectors.

Let rG=Q0.9({∥GiDP(α)−G¯DP(α)∥2}i=1N) r_G = Q_{0.9} \left( \left\{ \left\| G_i^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) - \overline G^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) \right\|_2 \right\}_{i=1}^{N} \right)

denote the empirical 90th percentile of the distances of the synthetic score points from their mean, and let

rH=max1≤j≤p∥HjDP(α)∥2. r_H = \max_{1\le j\le p} \left\| H_j^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) \right\|_2.

The common arrow scaling factor is

γ={rGrH,rG>0,rH>0,0,otherwise. \gamma = \begin{cases} \dfrac{r_G}{r_H}, & r_G>0,\ r_H>0,\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}

Therefore, the displayed variable vectors are H̃jDP(α)=γHjDP(α).\widetilde H_j^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha) = \gamma H_j^{\mathrm{DP}}(\alpha).

Ordinary reference. For comparison, non_private = TRUE asks the package to compute ordinary PCA from the sample covariance matrix. Let V̂\widehat V and λ̂ℓ\widehat\lambda_\ell be its directions and eigenvalues. Its scores are sample-mean centered, S=(X−𝟏nx‾⊤)V̂.S=(X-\mathbf1_n\bar x^\top)\widehat V.

4. Summary

Plot DP quantities used Interpretation
Scree / PVE λ̃1,…,λ̃k\widetilde\lambda_1,\ldots,\widetilde\lambda_k Shows the relative importance of the estimated PCs. PVE is normalized over the kk retained components.
Loading Ṽ\widetilde V Shows how the original variables contribute to the private PC directions.
Score F̃\widetilde F, h̃\widetilde h, and s1*,…,sN*s_1^*,\ldots,s_N^* Shows the distribution of projected observations without directly releasing their individual scores.
Variable Ṽk\widetilde V_k and λ̃1,…,λ̃k\widetilde\lambda_1,\ldots,\widetilde\lambda_k Shows relationships among variables implied by the private covariance approximation, rather than their exact empirical correlations.
Biplot Ṽ\widetilde V, λ̃1,…,λ̃k\widetilde\lambda_1,\ldots,\widetilde\lambda_k, and s1*,…,sN*s_1^*,\ldots,s_N^* Provides a joint view of the private score distribution and variable directions, with additional scaling for visualization.

The five DP PCA visualizations can be generated using dp_pca() and plot(), which reuse the estimated private quantities across the plots. For implementation details, plotting options, and examples, see the DP PCA Visualization Tutorial.
